[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Advanced Caching Strategies in Ruby on Rails"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Performance optimization is critical for scaling Ruby on Rails applications. As database queries and view rendering cycles multiply, caching becomes essential to reduce latency and server load. This tutorial explores three powerful caching techniques: Fragment Caching, Russian Doll Caching, and external memory stores like Redis and Memcached."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Fragment Caching"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Fragment caching allows you to isolate a portion of a view and cache it independently. Instead of caching an entire page, you cache specific components, such as a navigation bar, a user profile widget, or a product card in an e-commerce catalog."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"<% cache @product do %>

<%= @product.name %>

<%= number_to_currency(@product.price) %>

<% end %>"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"Rails automatically generates a cache key based on the object's model name and updated_at timestamp. When the product is updated, the timestamp changes, automatically invalidating the fragment cache."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Russian Doll Caching"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Russian Doll Caching involves nesting fragment caches inside one another. When an inner fragment changes, only that specific fragment is invalidated and recalculated, while the outer fragments remain cached. This requires careful handling of touch: true associations in your ActiveRecord models."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"# app/models/comment.rb class Comment < ApplicationRecord belongs_to :post, touch: true end"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"By adding touch: true to the Comment model, updating a comment will automatically update the parent Post's updated_at timestamp. Now, you can construct nested views efficiently."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"<% cache @post do %>

<%= @post.title %>

<%= render @post.comments %>
<% end %>"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Redis and Memcached Integration"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"While Rails defaults to memory store in development, production environments require robust out-of-process stores like Redis or Memcached. Redis is particularly powerful because it supports data persistence, complex data types, and pub/sub capabilities."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"# config/environments/production.rb config.cache_store = :redis_cache_store, { url: ENV.fetch("REDIS_URL") { "redis://localhost:6379/1" }, namespace: "my_app_production" }"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices and Summary"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always enable caching in development when testing performance features using bin/rails dev:cache."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use explicit cache keys or versioning when dealing with collections or complex queries that do not directly map to a single ActiveRecord model."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Monitor cache hit and miss ratios using your Redis or Memcached metrics dashboard to ensure your caching strategy is effective."}]
